name: Pumpkin seed oil

lead: Pumpkin seed oil, pressed from Cucurbita pepo seeds, is taken as an oral supplement or applied to the scalp by people hoping to slow or reverse male pattern hair loss and get thicker hair.

It is rich in unsaturated fatty acids, phytosterols and tocopherols, and phytosterols may weakly inhibit 5-alpha-reductase in laboratory studies. A 2014 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in men with androgenetic alopecia reported higher hair counts after 24 weeks, and a 2021 trial compared it with 5% minoxidil foam in women. Reviews describe these studies as small.

paras: It is usually taken as a daily capsule or oil, or used as a scalp product, often alongside approved treatments. Trial results were measured over about six months.
It is typically well tolerated, with occasional gastrointestinal upset or allergic reactions in people allergic to seeds. Product quality varies because it is sold as a food or supplement.

angle.text: Pumpkin seed oil is taken or applied for thicker scalp hair in male pattern hair loss. Its phytosterols may weakly reduce DHT activity at the follicle. A 2014 trial in men reported higher hair counts after 24 weeks, though studies are small.

lead: Pumpkin seed oil is a dark green to reddish culinary oil pressed from pumpkin seeds, associated especially with Styria in southeastern Austria and neighbouring parts of central and eastern Europe, and now also sold as an oral supplement and topical hair product [1][2]. It is rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids and contains phytosterols, tocopherols and squalene [2][3].

In appearance communities it is used as a natural option for slowing or reversing androgenetic alopecia, the common pattern of hair thinning, usually as a daily capsule and sometimes as a scalp oil. The chain people describe is: plant sterols and fatty acids may dampen the hormone pathway behind follicle shrinkage, thicker and more numerous hairs follow, and a fuller head of hair changes how the face and hairline look [4][5].

Human research exists and is small. A 2014 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 76 men with mild to moderate androgenetic alopecia reported a larger rise in hair count with oral pumpkin seed oil than with placebo over 24 weeks [4], and a 2021 randomised trial compared it with 5% minoxidil foam in 60 women with female pattern hair loss [6][7]. A 2026 systematic review and network meta-analysis of dietary supplements for androgenetic alopecia included it among supplements with a positive hair-density signal [8]. Reviews of natural products and supplements for hair loss describe the studies as small and preliminary and call for larger trials [9][10][11].
It is also studied for benign prostatic hyperplasia symptoms and cardiovascular outcomes in postmenopausal women [12][13][14][7].

paras: Wikipedia describes the oil as viscous and dichromatic: green in thin layers and red in thick ones. In twelve cultivars of Cucurbita maxima, linoleic acid made up about 36 to 63 percent of the oil, oleic acid 17 to 40 percent and palmitic acid 13 to 18 percent, with total unsaturated fatty acids of 73 to 81 percent [1].

Grokipedia, an AI-generated reference, adds that the Styrian hull-less seeds contain roughly 41 to 59 percent oil and that the oil contains tocopherols, phytosterols, carotenoids, phenolic compounds and squalene [2]. Production methods include cold pressing, roasting before pressing, solvent extraction and supercritical carbon dioxide extraction. Roasting before pressing is what gives Styrian oil its dark colour and nutty flavour [1][2].

According to Grokipedia, pumpkin seed records in Styria date to 1697, oil production to 1735, and a hull-less mutation of the Styrian oil pumpkin appeared around 1880, with systematic breeding from the 1930s; the oil was used in folk medicine for urinary and prostate complaints [2]. Grokipedia is AI-generated, so these dates are reported as stated there. Wikipedia places the culinary tradition in the former Austro-Hungarian region and notes that production has spread to new seed-growing areas, including China [1].

Its use for hair is more recent. The 2014 Korean trial by Cho and colleagues became the main citation for oral pumpkin seed oil in hair-loss discussions and in later reviews [4][9][10]. A 2019 mouse study reported that topical pumpkin seed oil partly reversed testosterone-induced hair-growth suppression [5].

The oil has an intense nutty flavour and is used as a salad dressing, on desserts such as vanilla ice cream, and a few drops in pumpkin soup; Wikipedia notes that heating it for cooking is said to destroy its essential fatty acids [1]. Styrian oil is made by pressing roasted seeds of the hull-less Styrian oil pumpkin [1]. Grokipedia gives a 2025 market size of about 1.25 billion US dollars [2].

Oral and topical pumpkin seed oil is marketed for hair growth in androgenetic alopecia. Reviews list it among natural products with clinical data, alongside saw palmetto, caffeine, melatonin and rosemary oil [9][15][16]. Grokipedia also mentions skin and acne uses, which it attributes to compositional rather than clinical evidence [2].
In hair-loss communities it is often discussed as a complement to, or alternative for, approved treatments, with some posters preferring it to minoxidil or finasteride for tolerability reasons [17].

Trials have examined pumpkin seed oil for benign prostatic hyperplasia symptoms, compared against tamsulosin and prazosin [12][13], and for arterial function and blood pressure in postmenopausal women [14][18][19].

The proposed mechanism for hair is inhibition of 5-alpha-reductase, the enzyme that converts testosterone into dihydrotestosterone (DHT), the hormone linked to follicle miniaturisation in androgenetic alopecia. The 2014 trial authors attribute this to phytosterols and base it mainly on earlier animal studies; they did not measure DHT or PSA, so the mechanism was not confirmed in participants [4].

A 2006 rat study found that oral pumpkin seed oil reduced testosterone-induced prostate enlargement, the basis for much of the 5-alpha-reductase hypothesis [7]. A 2019 mouse study from Iran applied 5% or 10% topical oil to testosterone-treated mice: the 10% preparation improved hair-growth scores and anagen follicle fraction (about 75 percent versus 44 percent with testosterone alone), while 2% minoxidil performed better (about 91 percent). The authors suggest fatty acids, beta-sitosterol, vitamin E and phytoestrogens may contribute and state the exact mechanism is unclear [5].

Tocopherols and squalene are proposed to have antioxidant effects, and Grokipedia reports in vitro antioxidant and antimicrobial activity [2][3]. A comprehensive review addresses the oil's composition, benefits and safety [3].

Male pattern hair loss: the 2014 trial (Cho and colleagues, Pusan National University hospitals, Korea) randomised 76 men aged 20 to 65 with mild to moderate androgenetic alopecia (Norwood II to V) to 400 mg of pumpkin seed oil daily or placebo for 24 weeks. Hair count measured by phototrichography rose 40 percent with pumpkin seed oil versus 10 percent with placebo; the mean change in count was 6.2 versus 1.8. Hair thickness did not differ between groups. Blinded photo assessment rated 44 percent of the oil group as improved versus 8 percent of the placebo group, and patient-reported improvement and satisfaction were higher at 24 weeks but not at 12 weeks [4].

The trial reported few adverse events and similar rates in both groups (itching in one participant per group and mild abdominal discomfort in one oil participant), stable liver enzymes and creatinine, and unchanged free testosterone. Its limitations, as stated by the authors, include no measurement of DHT, reliance on phototrichography and last-observation-carried-forward handling of dropouts; the capsule manufacturer funded the study and the authors called for replication [4].

Female pattern hair loss: a 2021 randomised comparative trial (Ibrahim and colleagues) assigned 30 women to pumpkin seed oil and 30 to minoxidil 5% foam for three months. Both treatments changed trichoscopic measures such as hair-shaft diversity and vellus hair counts, and upright regrowing hairs rose significantly with pumpkin seed oil; the authors concluded it shows promise [7].

Reviews: a 2023 JAMA Dermatology systematic review of nutritional supplements for hair loss in people without known deficiency included 17 randomised trials and other studies [10]. A 2022 review of natural products for male androgenetic alopecia identified 11 clinical studies and stated that pumpkin seed oil, among others, might be considered [9]. A 2026 network meta-analysis in Frontiers in Nutrition pooled 19 randomised trials with 1,658 participants across 16 supplements; it reported higher hair density with pumpkin seed oil than placebo (standardised mean difference 0.59, 95 percent confidence interval 0.09 to 1.09) but no significant benefit for terminal hair density, and its authors concluded that larger, higher-quality trials are needed and that evidence was not yet sufficient for direct clinical recommendations [8]. A review of topical alternatives found studies mostly small, often of combined formulations, with limited sample size and few comparisons with standard therapy [11]. Other reviews of herbal and complementary supplements are available [15][16][20].

Prostate: a 12-month randomised, double-blind trial in 47 Korean men with symptomatic BPH tested pumpkin seed oil, saw palmetto oil and both together; symptom scores fell in the single-oil and combination groups by three months, and prostate volume did not change [7]. Randomised trials also compared pumpkin seed oil with tamsulosin and with prazosin in symptomatic BPH [12][13]. Cardiovascular: randomised trials in postmenopausal women examined arterial hemodynamics and stiffness, and registered studies list blood pressure and menopausal symptoms as outcomes [14][18][19].

In the 2014 trial, adverse events were few and similar between groups [4]. The comprehensive review of the oil as a functional food covers safety [3]. Grokipedia describes the oil as generally recognised as safe by the FDA for food use, with rare mild gastrointestinal upset, and says patch testing is advised for people with seed allergies [2]. Reviews of natural hair products note that supplement quality varies [11]. The 2026 network meta-analysis reports that adverse events across supplements were mild, such as bloating, diarrhoea and itching, with mostly short-term safety data [8].

Styrian pumpkin seed oil carries a protected geographical indication in the European Union, granted in 1996 according to Grokipedia, and is a culinary specialty in Austria and Slovenia [1][2]. In North America and the UK it is mainly sold as a capsule or oil supplement for prostate and hair health.

In looksmaxxing and hair-loss communities, pumpkin seed oil is one of several natural options discussed alongside rosemary oil, saw palmetto, ketoconazole shampoo and peppermint oil. A looksmax.org thread asks whether it is "another cope" and reproduces an article citing the 2014 study, which the article describes as about 30 percent more hair growth than placebo [17]. The published trial reports a 40 percent hair-count increase versus 10 percent for placebo in 76 men [4]. The thread's quoted article also says the supplement was a multi-ingredient product; the published trial describes a single-ingredient pumpkin seed oil capsule [4][17].

Related approaches include saw palmetto, rosemary oil, caffeine shampoos and ketoconazole as natural or over-the-counter options, and finasteride and minoxidil as approved treatments for androgenetic alopecia [9][20]. The 2021 female trial directly compared pumpkin seed oil with minoxidil foam [7].
